extracted.intended_audience: literary critics, poets, and educated readers interested in the theory and practice of criticism and poetry
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative standards for the practice of literary criticism and for poets producing serious poetry—what criticism should aim to do and what poets must have to produce lasting work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criticism's aim: see the object as in itself it really is
rubrics_metrics.description: Criticism's business is, "in all branches of knowledge, theology, philosophy, history, art, science, to see the object as in itself it really is."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This means criticism should strive for an accurate, dispassionate apprehension of its subject; by doing so it establishes a clearer intellectual situation and an order of ideas which the creative power can profitably use. Criticism's mark is truthfulness of perception rather than party slant or practical utility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disinterestedness
rubrics_metrics.description: The rule for criticism may be summed up in one word,—"disinterestedness."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criticism must keep aloof from the "practical view of things" and refuse to lend itself to ulterior political or practical considerations. It should be a free play of the mind on its subjects, not a servant of sectional interests or immediate applications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Know the best that is known and thought in the world
rubrics_metrics.description: Criticism's business is "simply to know the best that is known and thought in the world, and by in its turn making this known, to create a current of true and fresh ideas."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critics should work with inflexible honesty and due ability to surface and disseminate the highest available ideas. The practical consequences of ideas are to be left to others; the critic's role is evaluative and clarifying, not instrumental.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criticism prepares the materials for creative genius
rubrics_metrics.description: The critical power, though lower in rank than the creative, tends to establish an order of ideas and to make the best ideas prevail; it prepares the intellectual atmosphere the creative power requires.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good criticism accumulates, purifies, and clarifies ideas so that a later creative epoch can arise; criticism therefore has an indispensable, preparatory historical function even if it ranks below invention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poets must know life and the world before dealing with them
rubrics_metrics.description: A poet ought to know life and the world before dealing with them in poetry; the creation of a modern poet, to be worth much, implies a great critical effort behind it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Creativity untutored by adequate knowledge or critical understanding results in works that are poor, barren, or short-lived (examples given: Byron's lack of endurance vs Goethe's lasting work). Poets need comprehensive and accurate materials drawn from a critical apprehension of life.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use ideas that are current at the time (materials must be ready)
rubrics_metrics.description: The elements with which the creative power works are ideas; they must be the best ideas "current at the time," not merely accessible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Literary genius primarily synthesizes and re-presents the intellectual atmosphere it finds itself in; without the contemporary 'moment' or circulating ideas, even great individual power cannot produce a master-work. Creators therefore depend on the quality and timeliness of the intellectual materials available to them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two kinds of dilettanti to avoid (Goethe)
rubrics_metrics.description: Goethe's two dilettanti in poetry: one who neglects the indispensable mechanical part and relies on spirituality/feeling; and one who seeks poetry merely by mechanism, acquiring artisan's readiness but "without soul and matter."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Both are faults: neglecting technique harms art, and reducing poetry to mere mechanism harms the individual. A sound poetic practice preserves both soul and technical mastery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respect for the practice of poetry; transmit regulative laws
rubrics_metrics.description: If we cannot attain the mastery of the great artists, "let us, at least, have so much respect for our art as to prefer it to ourselves" and "transmit to [successors] the practice of poetry, with its boundaries and wholesome regulative laws."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Writers should preserve and teach the craft's standards and limits so future excellence remains possible rather than be lost to caprice or neglect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Independent criticism (not organs of parties)
rubrics_metrics.description: There should be a criticism "absolutely and entirely independent" of sects and parties; organs of criticism that exist to serve political/religious fractions stifle free play of mind.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A criticism genuinely independent of party interests alone can attain real authority and create a current of true ideas. Examples contrast organs like the Revue des Deux Mondes (ideal) with partisan English reviews (Edinburgh, Quarterly, Times).

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid polemical practical criticism that fosters self-satisfaction
rubrics_metrics.description: Polemical, practical criticism subserving sectional interests makes men blind to ideal imperfection and leads to self-satisfaction that retards spiritual progression.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critics should resist converting evaluative thought into partisan defense or praise of current practice. Instead, criticism should highlight contrasts and imperfections to awaken moral and aesthetic reflection (example: juxtaposing eulogies of national perfection with a report of a child murder to show harsh realities).

rubrics_metrics.name: Creative excellence requires concurrence of man and moment
rubrics_metrics.description: For the creation of a master-work of literature two powers must concur: the power of the man and the power of the moment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Great works arise only when individual genius meets a receptive cultural/intellectual moment; authors should recognize the historic contingency of great creation and that preparation (critical work, learning) can make such concurrence more likely.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criticism can itself be a legitimate exercise of creative activity
rubrics_metrics.description: Though lower than invention, criticism may be an exercise of free creative activity and a source of personal fulfilment for many who cannot produce great works.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critics may attain a true happiness in critical practice; this validates criticism's cultural role and explains why many should and will pursue it rather than original composition.
